Finally, through multiple dataset-wide diagnostic analyses, we uncover key insights into model behavior, including the contribution of individual modalities across tasks and labels, spatial attribution patterns around target entities, and potential dataset biases. Overall, this work serves as both a benchmark and a practical guide for future XAI research in multimodal document understanding. To support reproducibility, we publicly release our code at https://github.com/saifullah3396/docxeval/.
items.title: DocXEval: A Systematic Evaluation of Explainability in Multimodal Document Understanding

items.summary: Face swapping transfers a source identity onto a target image while preserving the target's pose, expression, hair, and lighting. The most realistic current methods are diffusion-based, but they need many network evaluations per image. GAN-based methods are fast, yet trained from scratch they must learn realism from the adversarial signal alone and produce visibly weaker results. We present ALADDIN (Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping), a one-step face swapper obtained by initialising the generator from a pre-trained multi-step flow-matching model and training it adversarially under identity and target-preservation constraints. We expose a controllable trade-off between identity transfer and target-attribute preservation by training a student model with triplet pseudo-label supervision. We additionally identify a bias in the standard evaluation protocol, which favours methods trained against the same identity encoder used to score them, and re-evaluate all baselines with an independent one. ALADDIN is state-of-the-art among one-step methods in realism and target preservation at comparable identity transfer, and matches the best multi-step model with 28 times fewer network evaluations and an order of magnitude fewer training pairs.
items.title: ALADDIN: Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping

items.summary: For each time $t$, the regression function $m_t(x)=E[Y_t\mid X_t=x]$ of an outcome on contemporaneous covariates can be regarded as a field on covariate space. We study how this field evolves when the covariates of individual units move as a diffusion and the outcome attached to each unit changes according to its own dynamics. Under mild regularity we show that $m_t$ satisfies a second-order evolution equation whose diffusion term is $\frac12\mathrm{tr}(Σ\nabla^2 m_t)$, the trace of the Hessian of the regression function weighted by the instantaneous covariance $Σ$ of the covariate increments, whose transport term is the drift of the time-reversed covariate process, and whose source term is the conditional mean rate of change of the outcome. The equation is a regression-theoretic reading of a classical transport law, and it yields a Feynman-Kac representation of $m_t$ along reversed covariate paths. We connect the Hessian appearing in the equation to the Hessian estimated by quadratic regression (under Gaussian design the best quadratic approximation has Hessian $E[\nabla^2 m(X)]$ exactly) and to the leading bias of kernel smoothers. For binary outcomes governed by bistable replicator dynamics with imitation among units with similar covariates, the closed equation is of Nagumo type, its planar travelling fronts are exactly logistic in $(x,t)$, and a single logistic regression of the outcome on covariates and time identifies the ratio of diffusion to reaction and the direction of invasion. We discuss identification under panel versus repeated cross-sectional designs and a two-stage estimation strategy, and we illustrate the results with simulations.
items.title: Regression Functions as Fields on Covariate Space: Evolution Equations, the Hessian, and Identification

items.summary: Disasters are not merely natural phenomena; they are socially constructed events that emerge from the interaction between hazardous events and the vulnerable conditions of exposed communities. Floods, earthquakes, landslides, cyclones, wildfires, droughts, and extreme weather events continue to cause widespread human, material, economic, and environmental losses across the globe. As climate change intensifies hazard events, urbanization concentrates populations in vulnerable areas, and technological systems become increasingly complex and interdependent, the need for sophisticated disaster management capabilities has never been greater. This book explores the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in disaster management. It examines how AI technologies—including machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, robotics, and expert systems—are being applied across all phases of the disaster management cycle: mitigation, preparedness, response, and recovery. The integration of AI with remote sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, cloud computing, and real-time analytics offers unprecedented opportunities for predicting, preparing for, responding to, and recovering from disasters. The book is organized into eleven chapters that progressively build the reader's understanding of this interdisciplinary field. Chapter 1 establishes the foundational concepts of disasters, the disaster management cycle, and the evolution of disaster management technologies. Chapter 2 introduces the fundamentals of AI, machine learning, deep learning, and neural network architectures, with a focus on their relevance to disaster applications. Chapter 3 examines AI based disaster risk assessment and hazard mapping, integrating geospatial information,  environmental observations, and computational models. Chapters 4 through 8 address specific disaster types: floods, earthquakes, landslides, cyclones and extreme weather events, and wildfires, droughts, and climate-related disasters. Each chapter presents AI applications, case studies, numerical examples, and integrated frameworks tailored to the unique characteristics of these hazards. Chapter 9 explores the synergy between remote sensing, GIS, and AI for disaster mapping and damage assessment. Chapter 10 focuses on IoT, sensors, and real-time AI-based disaster monitoring, emphasizing edge computing, cloud platforms, and early-warning systems. Chapter 11 presents an integrated AI framework, case studies from India and internationally, performance evaluation metrics, challenges, research gaps, and future directions.    Throughout the book, a critical distinction is maintained: AI should not be viewed as a replacement for human judgment, field observations, engineering expertise, or disaster management experience. Rather, AI serves as a powerful complement—augmenting human capabilities, improving the speed and consistency of information processing, and supporting evidence-based forecasting, monitoring, response, and recovery. The most effective disaster management architecture integrates AI with hydrological and hydraulic modelling, seismology, structural engineering, geotechnical engineering, meteorological science, and institutional decision-making. The book emphasizes several cross-cutting themes. First, the relationship between hazard, vulnerability, exposure, and risk provides the analytical foundation for disaster risk assessment. The formula Risk = (Hazard × Vulnerability × Exposure) / Capacity demonstrates that risk can be reduced through strategic interventions that decrease vulnerability and exposure or increase capacity. Second, data quality, algorithmic bias, infrastructure requirements, trust deficits,  privacy concerns, capacity gaps, interoperability problems, and regulatory uncertainty must all be addressed for AI to achieve its full potential. items.title: AI IN DISASTER MANAGEMENT

items.summary: We develop a multifidelity black-box variational inference (MF-BBVI) approach for PDE-constrained Bayesian inverse problems in which forward solves are expensive and PDE gradients are unavailable. The method is built on score-function estimators for the evidence lower bound (ELBO), which avoid differentiation through the PDE model but are known to suffer from high variance. To address this high variance, we employ multifidelity approximate control-variate estimators that combine a small number of high-fidelity samples with a larger number of low-fidelity samples to reduce estimator variance and the number of high-fidelity evaluations required for optimization. We further develop a PDE-derivative-free second-order optimization strategy based on both gradient and Hessian score-function estimators. For low-fidelity model generation, we propose an on-the-fly strategy that builds and adaptively updates a reduced-order model (ROM) as the variational distribution evolves throughout the optimization. We investigate strategies for adapting the ROM and estimating the approximate control-variate gains, examining tradeoffs between estimator bias, variance reduction, and computational cost. The resulting approach facilitates derivative-free variational inference for large-scale inverse problems through a reduction in overall computational cost. We demonstrate the method on four numerical examples: a linear benchmark with an exact posterior and three PDE-constrained inverse problems.
items.title: Multifidelity variational inference for derivative-free PDE-constrained inverse problems

items.summary: Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation (OSTTA) operates on non-stationary target streams where covariate and semantic shifts coexist. Existing TTA methods often obtain adaptation signals by updating model parameters or maintaining mutable memories, which can be costly and vulnerable to unknown samples. We present TALOR, a lightweight, backward-free rectification module that uses the source linear head as a geometric anchor. The head-induced basis decomposes each normalized feature into high-gain principal coordinates and low-gain tail coordinates. TALOR estimates a soft-routed affine correction in the principal subspace, combining a regime-level principal bias with a tail-conditioned slope that captures sample-level tail-to-principal coupling. Using weighted ridge regression, it subtracts this drift estimate from the principal coordinates, reconstructs the feature and feeds it into the source head. On the ImageNet-C benchmark with six csOOD datasets, TALOR outperforms the next-best UniEnt by 2.2% H-score while running 2.5x faster and using only 12% of its GPU memory; as a post-correction plug-in, it further boosts COME to 68.4% H-score with only 2% additional memory overhead.
items.title: Tail Cues, Principal Corrections: Plug-and-Play Rectification for Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation
